text: The Archives New Zealand building in the capital city of Wellington is so ordinary-looking that most local people are unaware of its function. It houses the country's vast quantity of government documents and information relating to all aspects of New Zealand's past. Now these documents have become even more accessible. This is because since 2005, Archway, an online database, has enabled visitors to the Archives New Zealand website to search approximately two million records from 4,000 government agencies. Type in, for example, 'Denniston Mine Railway' and you'll be presented with a list of documents, files and plans from 1878 onwards relating to the construction and use of the rail line. There's even video footage of it from a 1967 documentary. Though the actual records are not online, copies can usually be obtained from the relevant Archives office.

text: In the past, New Zealand was careless about preserving its past. Documents were either thrown out or stored in the damp basements of buildings. Accidents made the problem worse. In 1862, a ship carrying early government records sank off the coast of Wellington. In 1957, various records were badly damaged by fire. Much of the burnt paper has been kept in the hope that advances in preservation technology will enable future archivists to restore the material. The fire provided the motivation for setting up Archives New Zealand and taking greater care of historical documents.

text: Most documents relating to property ownership are held by Land Information New Zealand (LINZ), which is in the process of digitising its massive collection for its own database. The originals will then be transferred to Archives New Zealand, which already holds about 85 kilometres of records, says Dianne Macaskill, chief archivist and chief executive of Archives New Zealand. The LINZ records will increase the size of the collection of archived documents by about a third. Archives New Zealand is also digitising some of its own material so it can be accessed more easily, says Macaskill. However, with more than five million items, many of varying shape and size, digitisation is likely to be labour-intensive and hugely expensive.

text: Though every item is carefully filed and can be quickly retrieved, the search for particular information can still be like a treasure hunt and present an interesting challenge for archivists. It's a bit like being a detective and following the clues, because one particular topic might be in a number of different places.

text: These days, Archives New Zealand hosts a number of permanent exhibitions. Some of these include letters and diaries written by a number of the country's politicians going back for many years.
